title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Oil & Gas
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Peninsula Energy confirms the cyberattack on its Wyoming uranium project hit well-field and plant control systems; the site is shut down
items.content_text: Peninsula Energy said on 25 November that the cyber incident found at its Lance uranium in-situ recovery project in Crook County, Wyoming, on 20 November reached the plant and well-field operating and control systems, not only business IT. The site has been shut down while investigation and recovery run, and the ASX-listed producer’s shares stay suspended until 30 November. Its first disclosure said US and Australian administrative systems were not affected. Peninsula has not named an attacker, described the entry route or given a restart date, and no group has claimed the attack. In-situ recovery runs injection and production wells, header houses and a central plant under remote SCADA, much like an upstream oil field, making this the closest confirmed OT-disruptive incident to oil and gas operations this month (editorial assessment).

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story
_otthreatfeed.source_name: Discovery Alert (25 Nov 2026, Peninsula Energy market update); SecurityWeek (24 Nov 2026, first disclosure and trading halt); cross-sector item — oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment

items.title: Coast Guard confirms cyber boardings of US-bound ships as officials weigh Iran’s role in up to 50 attacks on oil, LNG and chemical tankers
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard has confirmed that its cyber teams boarded US-bound ships to investigate cyber incidents, while declining to discuss specific attacks, after the Wall Street Journal reported on 23 November that US officials see Iran as the main suspect in as many as 50 cyberattacks on tankers carrying oil, liquefied gas and chemicals. Teams went to at least four vessels nearing US shores, including the Texas-bound VL Prosperity, whose captain received a ransom note, and the Kohaku. Other targeted ships were near Europe and Asia, and some crews did not know they had been hit. Some officials also point to Russia, one called four of the attacks a minor nuisance, no ship is reported disabled, and Iran denies involvement. Export terminals, LNG berths and loading jetties sit at the shore end of these links (editorial assessment).

items.title: Norway ties the Equinor and Skagerak Energi intrusions to a flaw in Microsoft’s Azure API Management; Equinor’s oil and gas production ran normally throughout
items.content_text: Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said on 20 November that an unidentified actor exploited a flaw in Classic tiers of Microsoft’s Azure API Management (APIM) to reach stored secrets: named values, identity-provider client secrets, subscription keys and management API tokens. Equinor and Skagerak Energi were among several organisations hit. Equinor detected its intrusion on 17 November and contained it on 20 November; some internal services were disrupted, but oil and gas production ran normally and it sees no sign data was stolen or altered. Skagerak’s operations were also unaffected. Microsoft found the flaw on 18 November and closed the access path on 19 November; no CVE has been issued. NSM advises treating APIM secrets as compromised and rotating them. Nothing points to OT, but cloud API gateways carrying production or trading data are attack surface (editorial assessment).

items.title: SAP investigates a breach that German media say reached its GitHub source code, raising supply-chain questions for refiners and pipelines that run on SAP
items.content_text: SAP says it is investigating a cybersecurity incident after detecting suspicious activity and has so far found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data. Der Spiegel, citing insiders, reports that attackers stole employees’ GitHub authentication tokens and used them to copy and alter source code; Handelsblatt says SAP replaced signing keys, restricted GitHub access and paused automated development. It is not clear whether proprietary code was touched, and no report says altered code reached customers. A late-October leak-site claim by The Gentlemen ransomware group does not appear to be connected. Refiners, pipeline operators and producers commonly tie SAP to plant maintenance, work orders and hydrocarbon accounting, so the integrity of SAP updates and connectors matters on the operations side (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw, CVE-2026-123039, to become root. They deployed web shells and backdoors, moved to a VMware ESXi host over SSH and ran a wiper that zeroes files. The first wave hit Israeli organisations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries and sectors without destruction. Check Point cannot attribute it with confidence; the backdoors resemble tooling linked to China-nexus UNC5221. CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No oil and gas victim is reported, but these gateways often front plant remote access and ESXi often hosts HMIs and historians (editorial assessment).

items.title: N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after miners turned up on patched servers, then discloses a breach of its hosted email-filtering cloud
items.content_text: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November as a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. It followed Huntback’s finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them already on Hotfix 2. On-premises servers need the upgrade now, and every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes. Separately, N-able said on 20 November that attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts cloud; it says mail flow continued, no access to customer data was found and N-central is unrelated. Integrators often manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools (editorial assessment).

items.title: Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority forces manual workarounds at Latin America’s busiest port
items.content_text: The Port of Santos authority, which runs Brazil’s largest port, lost its IT systems on 6 November and confirmed a cyberattack on 10 November. Access-control systems and digital tools for coordinating port operations went down, delaying vessel, truck and train procedures and forcing some checks, such as matching ship dimensions to berths, to be done by hand. By 16 November core internal systems were in final tests and about 70% of affected file backups had been recovered; ship movements and landside access continued throughout. Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating; the attacker and entry route are undisclosed. For fuel and liquid-bulk terminals inside a port, the lesson is to know how berthing and gate access work when the authority’s systems are down (editorial assessment).

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US energy, water and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localised, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing, officials said they found no evidence that hackers caused the Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions. AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups passing network access to one another, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For oil and gas, the weakest exposed controllers are the target (editorial assessment).

items.title: FBI warns the ARTEX autonomous AI pentest framework is being used in real intrusions, some reaching privileged access in under three hours, with energy on the target list
items.content_text: The FBI issued FLASH-20261113-001 on 13 November, warning that threat actors are using ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework written in Go, to automate reconnaissance, exploitation and exfiltration; some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours. ARTEX turns natural-language objectives into commands and plugs into outside AI models. Its developer pulled the GitHub repository on 8 October, but forks, mirrors and a commercial version keep it available, and researchers counted more than 1,600 exposed consoles in early November. The FBI lists energy among targeted sectors and names the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain compromise among ARTEX campaigns. Initial access comes through web-application flaws, weak or hard-coded credentials, abused vendor trust and stolen VPN configurations. Texas regulators cited the FLASH on 18 November (see Regulation & Policy).

items.title: GreyNoise: an AI-assisted crew it tracks as GT13 broke into Check Point Security Management servers at 22 or more organisations, energy companies among them
items.content_text: GreyNoise researchers say a crew they track as GT13 used AI-assisted tooling to breach Check Point Security Management servers at no fewer than 22 organisations, including energy, transport and manufacturing companies, in activity running from 17 October to 2 November; Cybersecurity Dive reported the findings on 24 November. A management server holds the policy, objects and administrator access for every gateway it controls, so one compromise reaches each firewall in the estate. Victims were not named, and the reporting does not say whether any oil and gas operator was hit or whether the crew moved into plant networks. This sits beside the PHP2Shell exploitation of Check Point gateways (see Incidents & Attacks). A single console managing IT/OT boundary firewalls is a crown-jewel asset (editorial assessment).

items.title: Switzerland confirms its first AI-agent cyberattacks: four of five succeeded, with power, water and telecom operators among the targets
items.content_text: Switzerland’s Federal Office for Cybersecurity (BACS) said on 26 November that five attacks in recent days used AI agents, frameworks that find weaknesses, pick tools and plan next steps largely on their own. Four of the five compromised systems. Three targets were critical-infrastructure operators, which public broadcaster SRF identified as electricity, water and telecommunications providers; no oil or gas company was named. BACS named no victims or attacker and has not said whether any control systems were reached. The entry points were ordinary: default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in internet-facing systems, the pattern the UK NCSC described on 24 November. Remote well pads, compressor stations and terminals with exposed HMIs, modems and VPNs fit that profile (editorial assessment).

items.title: Dragos counts 47 ransomware attacks on oil and gas organisations in Q3 among 1,266 industrial cases, and saw no operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organisations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, and counted 47 oil and natural gas incidents across upstream, midstream, downstream and service providers. Among them, The Gentlemen listed Argentina’s Oldelval, which runs the main crude pipeline network out of Vaca Muerta, on 23 July; Oldelval said only administrative systems were affected and crude transport continued. Cl0p claimed Shell among its victims, a claim Dragos has not verified. Qilin and The Gentlemen led overall. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: disruption came through the IT, ERP and virtualisation layers plants depend on. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials.

items.title: Trellix counts about 1,500 ransomware leak-site posts against industrial sectors in six months, up 50.8% quarter on quarter, and puts energy and oil and gas second in its OT telemetry
items.content_text: Trellix’s November OT Threat Report, covering April to September 2026, counts about 1,500 ransomware leak-site posts naming organisations in manufacturing, construction, transportation and warehousing, mining and oil and gas extraction, and utilities, up 50.8% quarter on quarter. Manufacturing accounts for about two-thirds and utilities under 2%; The Gentlemen and Qilin lead with about 16% each. In Trellix’s own product telemetry, energy and oil and gas make up 12.3% of OT-sector activity, second only to manufacturing at 49.3%; those shares measure product activity, not confirmed compromises. Trellix says the enterprise-edge exploitation it tracked did not establish a path into ICS networks. For oil and gas, the pressure stays on the IT and edge layers that production, scheduling and custody transfer depend on (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell: Schneider’s Foxboro DCS H90 Server still has no fix, and Siemens and ABB keep adding grid-control, RTU and gateway products
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified research by Dream showing a suspected China-nexus actor chaining the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials; Check Point gateways were later hit too (see Incidents & Attacks). OT vendors keep finding the same PHP code in their products. Schneider Electric lists the EcoStruxure Foxboro DCS H90 Server with no fix, mitigation only. Siemens lists Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways; ABB lists Netcontrol RTUs and ASPECT gateways, several unfixed. None of the OT products is reported exploited and no oil and gas operator is named. Foxboro DCS is widely used in refining and gas processing (editorial assessment).

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported it, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited it for more than two months beforehand: it got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, attacked vCenter in early September, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 20 November. No victims or sectors are named. Many refineries and gas plants run HMIs, historians and engineering workstations as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment).

items.title: Siemens: the Node2Shell Brotli flaw reaches WinCC, WinCC OA and TIA tools, and an NTLM relay weakness hits PCS 7 and Process Historian with no fix planned
items.content_text: Siemens published two advisories on 10 November that CISA republished on 17 November. SSA-242944 (ICSA-26-321-03) covers CVE-2026-111497, the Brotli decoder buffer overflow behind October’s Node.js “Node2Shell” updates, scored CVSS 9.8: a crafted compressed stream can corrupt memory and potentially run code. Fixes exist for WinCC OA V3.20 (P17.1), Braumat and Sistar; WinCC V7/V8, WinCC OA V3.21, WinCC Unified, TIA Administrator and UMC have mitigations only. SSA-970803 (ICSA-26-321-08) describes an NTLM relay weakness, CVSS 7.5, that lets an on-path attacker impersonate users; no fix is planned for PCS 7 V9.1, Batch V9.1, Process Historian or Information Server, and none is available yet for WinCC. CISA added the Brotli CVE to KEV on 27 October. WinCC OA is common in pipeline SCADA and PCS 7 in refineries and petrochemical plants (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, began within two days of its 17 November disclosure; GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November, and none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups. For OT teams the key item is Siemens SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched. Engineering teams at plants often run Jira, Jenkins and Keycloak beside OT tooling (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
items.content_text: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organisation, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network and gained root. From there they ran Python scripts, which F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing, to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 20 November alongside the vCenter zero-day. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported, but Expressway is a perimeter gateway that bridges outside callers into internal networks, so an exposed, unpatched cluster is a foothold close to plant-side systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: AutomationDirect C-More EA9 programming software: a crafted project file can trigger a heap overflow and run code on the engineering workstation
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-328-01 on 24 November for AutomationDirect’s C-More EA9 HMI programming software, versions 6.80 and earlier. CVE-2026-127280 (CVSS 7.8) is a heap-based buffer overflow: if a user opens a maliciously crafted project file, an attacker could execute arbitrary code on the workstation running the software. It needs that user action, and CISA reports no known public exploitation. The advisory lists critical manufacturing, energy and water among the sectors using the product. C-More touch panels are common on integrator-built skids, compressor packages, tank-farm and wellsite control panels, so project files swapped with contractors and OEMs are the realistic delivery route (editorial assessment).

items.title: Texas Railroad Commissioner urges oil, gas and pipeline operators to harden now, citing the FBI’s ARTEX warning and the recent wave of outages
items.content_text: Railroad Commission of Texas Commissioner Wayne Christian again urged oil and gas producers, pipeline operators and other Texas energy companies on 18 November to bolster their cyber defences, saying the state’s energy infrastructure “is undoubtedly a target” and that operators cannot wait until an attack halts it. He pointed to the FBI’s 13 November FLASH on the ARTEX AI framework, which lists energy among targeted sectors (see Threat Intelligence & Research), and to recent widespread outages, while noting ARTEX may not be the only explanation; federal officials have said they found no evidence of hacking in those outages. He asked companies to find and fix vulnerabilities, secure their networks, monitor for suspicious activity and prepare a response plan before an attack. It is a call to action, not a new RRC rule.

items.title: France expects EU sanctions on 14 December against those behind October’s refrigeration sabotage, which Paris blames on an IRGC unit
items.content_text: France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said on 17 November that he expects EU foreign ministers to agree sanctions on 14 December against the individuals behind October’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration controllers, freezing their assets and barring them from the EU, a day after EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said new Iran sanctions were being prepared. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit for the attack on about 700 French sites, which French authorities say caused at least 15 fires, and has sought arrest warrants for three officers. Iran rejects the accusations, and the attribution has not been independently confirmed. For oil and gas, the case shows a state actor willing to cause physical effects through exposed industrial controllers, the same pattern suspected in the tanker breaches (see Incidents & Attacks; editorial assessment).

items.title: Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of its OT security guide, the reference many auditors and insurers use alongside API 1164 and IEC 62443
items.content_text: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for building automation, water, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels and cloud-connected industrial IoT. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions and applying zero-trust principles. Oil and gas gets no new dedicated section, but regulators, insurers and auditors often cite 800-82 alongside API 1164 and IEC 62443, so its final wording can shape what pipeline, refinery and terminal operators are asked to show (editorial assessment). The window closes in three days.
